title: Fix nonzero exit on child process crash
body:
## Motivation

When a scheduler or other child process crashes, the tokenizer manager receives `SIGQUIT` and tears down the process tree. Previously, `kill_process_tree()` always exited the current process with status code `0`, so Kubernetes could treat child process failures, including CUDA illegal memory access crashes, as successful exits.

This makes failures harder to detect in production because the container may terminate with a misleading success status.

## Modifications

- Add an `exit_code` argument to `kill_process_tree()`, defaulting to `0` to preserve existing behavior.
- Pass `exit_code=1` from `TokenizerManager`'s running-phase `SIGQUIT` handler, since this path usually means a child process failed.
- Add unit tests covering the default exit code and the overridden non-zero exit code behavior.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable. This PR does not affect model outputs, kernels, sampling, or forward computation.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable. This PR only changes process teardown behavior on failure paths and has no expected impact on inference performance.

title: [hicache] Fix hf3fs extra (non-KV) pool page size
body:
## Problem
`HiCacheHF3FS.register_mem_host_pool_v2` sizes each extra (non-KV) pool with
`get_ksize_per_token() * page_size` (K only). But `_pool_batch_set` writes one
combined K+V page per key (`get_data_page(flat=True)`) and `_pool_batch_get`
reads into `get_dummy_flat_data_page()` of that same combined size. So the K-only
`bytes_per_page` under-counts the real page: per-page offsets and `num_pages` are
wrong and the write trips `Hf3fsClient.check` (`size > bytes_per_page`), crashing
the backup thread so nothing is persisted to L3.

The KV pool is unaffected because it is zero-copy split into separate `-k`/`-v`
keys, so its per-entry write equals the K-only size. The bug surfaces on hybrid
models that register an extra pool (e.g. SWA) with `--hicache-storage-backend hf3fs`.

## Fix
Size each extra pool from `get_dummy_flat_data_page()` — the exact buffer the
read/write path uses — so `bytes_per_page`, offsets, `num_pages` and the size
check all match the real I/O.

## Verification
Verified end-to-end on an internal hybrid-SWA setup (TP=4) with hicache L3=hf3fs:
after the fix the extra pool registers the correct `bytes_per_page`, and a
write_through + flush + replay cycle shows `backuped_tokens_total` and
`prefetched_tokens_total` both increasing with `cache_source=storage_HiCacheHF3FS`.

title: fix: restore DP-attention shm barrier in SchedulerRequestReceiver los…
body:
…t during #25610 refactor

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Problem

After PR #25610 refactored request-ingress logic from `scheduler.py` into
`SchedulerRequestReceiver`, the DP-attention barrier originally introduced
by PR #23027 was not carried over to the new location.

This causes `FileNotFoundError: /psm_xxxxxxxx` when running:
- Multimodal model (e.g. Kimi-K2.5)
- PD disaggregation (`event_loop_overlap_disagg_prefill`)
- `dp_size > 1` + `--enable-dp-attention`

**Stack trace:**
```
event_loop_overlap_disagg_prefill
  → request_receiver.recv_requests()
  → _broadcast_reqs_across_ranks → broadcast_pyobj (attn_tp_cpu_group)
      → pickle.loads → __setstate__ → shm_open
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/psm_xxxxxxxx'
```

## Root Cause

`_finalize_shm_features` only adds a barrier for the non-DP-attention path.
The comment states "under DP-attention no barrier is needed because the
subsequent `control_reqs` broadcast on `tp_cpu_group` acts as an implicit barrier."

However, in the `disagg_prefill` code path there is **no** subsequent
`control_reqs` broadcast, so the assumption does not hold. The source rank
(TP0) races ahead from `broadcast_pyobj` to `unwrap_shm_features →
materialize → shm_unlink` before receiver ranks (TP1+) have completed
`pickle.loads → shm_open`.

## Fix

Add an `elif` branch in `_finalize_shm_features` that explicitly barriers
on `attn_tp_cpu_group` (and `attn_cp_cpu_group` if CP is enabled) for the
DP-attention case, symmetric with the existing `tp_cpu_group` barrier for
the non-DP-attention path.

## Verification

Verified on Kimi-K2.5, PD disaggregation, dp_size=2, tp_size=8,
`--enable-dp-attention`. Previously crashed within minutes; no crash
observed after applying this fix.

## Related

- Fixes the root cause described in #23022
- PR #23027 attempted the same fix targeting `scheduler.py`, but became
  conflicted after #25610 moved the code to `request_receiver.py`

title: Fix FP4 KV cache for Qwen3.6 hybrid linear pools
body:
## Summary

This updates FP4 KV cache support for Qwen3.6 hybrid linear-attention models so decode can consume packed FP4 KV buffers directly instead of falling back to full-pool dequantization.

## Changes

- Select `MHATokenToKVPoolFP4` for non-MLA hybrid full-attention layers when the requested KV dtype is `torch.float4_e2m1fn_x2`.
- Expose raw packed FP4 K/V buffers and scale buffers from `MHATokenToKVPoolFP4`, and forward those accessors through `HybridLinearKVPool` with the full-attention layer-id mapping.
- Add a Triton FP4 decode attention path that unpacks E2M1 FP4 KV values and applies the block scale inside the decode kernel.
- Route Triton decode through the FP4 path when the token-to-KV pool supports it, while keeping the existing decode path for FP8/BF16/MLA.
- Keep the `KVFP4QuantizeUtil` compatibility name for FP4 KV memory-pool users.
- Avoid deriving `v_head_dim` through `get_value_buffer(0)` when the backing pool exposes `v_head_dim` or `kv_lora_rank`, which avoids accidental FP4 pool dequantization.

## Validation

- `python3 -m py_compile python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/triton_ops/decode_attention.py python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/triton_backend.py python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py python/sglang/srt/layers/quantization/kvfp4_tensor.py`
- `git diff --check`

title: Fix processor BOS/EOS compatibility restoration
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

Transformers v5 may drop `add_bos_token` and `add_eos_token` settings when
loading a tokenizer backed by `tokenizer.json`. It assumes that the serialized
tokenizer post-processor already handles BOS/EOS insertion, but that is not true
for every tokenizer configuration.

SGLang already compensates for this behavior in `get_tokenizer()` by reading
`tokenizer_config.json`, restoring the supported flags, and rebuilding the
tokenizer post-processor.

SGLang has two related loading entry points:

- `get_tokenizer()` returns a tokenizer directly and is typically used by
  text-only loading paths.
- `get_processor()` returns a multimodal processor that owns a tokenizer in
  addition to image, audio, or other preprocessing components.

Both entry points ultimately tokenize the text portion of a request, so their
tokenizer compatibility behavior should be consistent. Before this change,
only the direct `get_tokenizer()` path applied the Transformers-v5 BOS/EOS
repair. The tokenizer embedded in a processor bypassed it.

This does not affect every model. The compatibility helper is limited to
tokenizer classes that supported these flags before Transformers v5, currently
including Llama, Code Llama, Gemma, and Cohere tokenizers. It is a no-op for
other tokenizer classes and for configurations whose values are already
correct.

Multimodal models commonly load the same tokenizer through `get_processor()`.
That path extracts the processor-owned tokenizer and applies several post-load
fixes, but it does not apply the existing BOS/EOS compatibility repair. The same
checkpoint can therefore tokenize a prompt differently depending on which
loading entry point is used. For affected Gemma tokenizers, the processor path
can omit the expected BOS token.

This change does not alter Transformers itself or introduce a new compatibility
policy. It applies SGLang's existing policy consistently to the tokenizer owned
by a processor.

## Modifications

- Apply the existing `_fix_v5_add_bos_eos_token()` helper to the final tokenizer
  selected by `get_processor()`.
- Keep the compatibility policy in one place rather than duplicating it in the
  processor loader.
- Add a CPU-only regression test that loads a local Gemma tokenizer
  configuration through the processor path and verifies that `add_bos_token`
  is restored and the tokenizer post-processor is rebuilt.

The helper already limits restoration to tokenizer classes that supported
these flags before Transformers v5. Unsupported tokenizer classes and
tokenizers with correct settings remain unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

This changes tokenizer initialization rather than model execution. The added
CPU regression test verifies the affected tokenization state without model
weights or accelerator hardware.

- Focused unit test: pending GitHub CI.
- Python syntax check: passed.
- `black --check`: passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable. The compatibility repair runs once while loading a processor
and does not affect the inference hot path.

title: Detokenizer: call the tokenizers backend decode directly instead of HF batch_decode for stock fast tokenizers
body:
## Motivation

The per-row Python wrapper around tokenizer decoding dominates the fast-tokenizer path. At batch size 256, CPU profiling of the real `_decode_batch_token_id_output` shows only ~14% of profiled time inside `tokenizers.Tokenizer.decode`, with most of the cost coming from the Python `batch_decode` wrapper.

For the standard `TokenizersBackend` configuration, where `batch_decode` and `_decode` have not been overridden or patched and the underlying tokenizer is a `tokenizers.Tokenizer`, bypass the Python `batch_decode` wrapper and call the backend decoder directly for each row.

The fast path uses a bound local `backend.decode` and preserves the existing `skip_special_tokens` behavior. All other tokenizer implementations and customized methods continue to use the existing `batch_decode` path.

## Modifications

- Detect the standard `TokenizersBackend` configuration once at initialization using function identity.
- In the fast path and grouped decoding path, replace `batch_decode` with:
  `backend.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=skip)` for each non-empty row.
- Keep the existing `batch_decode` path for:
  - slow tokenizers
  - tiktoken
  - Mistral/custom tokenizer implementations
  - subclasses overriding `_decode`
  - patched or otherwise customized tokenizer methods
- Preserve existing empty-row filtering and grouped-result scattering.
- Do not use `tokenizers` parallel `decode_batch`, which was slower at the target batch sizes.

## Accuracy Tests

**Passed**: Correctness verification completed.

- All relevant detokenizer manager unit tests passed.
- Baseline and candidate outputs are identical across 300-step streams.
- Tested batch sizes 1, 64, and 256.
- Tested Gemma-2 tokenizer with regular README text token IDs and special token IDs `0/1/2/106/107`.
- Tested mixed `skip_special_tokens` and `spaces_between_special_tokens` settings.
- Tested stop-string completion.
- Tested multi-byte UTF-8 sequences split across tokens, including replacement-character behavior.
- Verified that slow tokenizers and subclasses overriding `_decode` take the existing fallback path.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Performance improvement measured and verified on NVIDIA B300 SXM6.

| Arm | n | Median | Unit |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Baseline | 10 | 1189.92 | us per step |
| Candidate | 10 | 619.982 | us per step |

- Ratio: 0.5210

The optimization reduces the measured detokenization step from ~1.19 ms to ~0.62 ms at batch size 256.

title: TokenizerManager: hoist weight_version lookup out of request loop
body:
reduce calling self.config_value("weight_version") to 1, from `batch_size`
## Motivation

`_handle_batch_output` previously called `self.config_value("weight_version")` for every request in the batch. For large batches, this repeated lookup adds unnecessary CPU overhead in the tokenizer/HTTP process.

Hoist the lookup above the request loop and reuse the value for all rows in the batch.

This also makes the reported `weight_version` consistent across a batch. Previously, rows processed after an `await asyncio.sleep(0)` could observe a `weight_version` update that occurred during batch processing. With this change, all rows report the value observed at batch start.

Per-token weight-version attribution remains available separately through `recv_obj.weight_versions` and `add_weight_versions_to_meta_info`.

The single-request abort path is unchanged.

## Modifications

- Read `weight_version` once before iterating over `recv_obj.rids`.
- Reuse the local value when constructing `meta_info`.
- No other behavior or output processing is changed.

## Accuracy Tests

Verified baseline and candidate using identical `BatchStrOutput` sequences covering:

- Streaming and non-streaming outputs
- Incremental and non-incremental outputs
- Finished rows
- Weight-version updates between batches

All relevant unit tests pass, including tokenizer manager configuration update, RID cleanup, multi-tokenizer, and server-info tests.

The resulting `state.out_list` entries are equivalent across baseline and candidate for the tested cases, including `meta_info["weight_version"]` updates between batches.

The intended semantic difference is limited to a `weight_version` update occurring during processing of a single batch: the candidate consistently reports the batch-start value for all rows.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Measured `handle_batch_output_ms` on NVIDIA B300 SXM6 PC x1 using CUDA-event timing.

10 trials per arm after 2 warmup trials, interleaved ABBA. Lower is better.

| Arm | n | Median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Baseline | 10 | 0.798548 ms |
| Candidate | 10 | 0.480144 ms |

This corresponds to a **39.87% reduction** in `_handle_batch_output` time (`0.6013x` baseline).

At batch size 256, this represents approximately 0.2 ms saved per batch output.

The optimization primarily removes repeated `config_value("weight_version")` calls. The absolute benefit depends on how much `_handle_batch_output` is dominated by this lookup versus metrics, logprob handling, and other per-request work.

No end-to-end throughput improvement is claimed.

title: memoize stop-string tail decoding within a step
body:
## Motivation

`Req.tail_str` can be called multiple times for the same request step, including during finish checks and streaming prefix checks. Cache the decoded tail string using `(len(output_ids), tail_len)` as the key so identical decodes within a step are performed only once.

The key changes when tokens are appended, retracted/reset, or multiple speculative tokens are accepted, so no explicit invalidation is required in those cases. When `output_ids` is rewritten in place without changing its length, clear the memo explicitly before finishing the request.

## Modifications

- Memoize the most recently decoded tail string in `Req`.
- Key the cache by `(len(output_ids), tail_len)`.
- Reuse the cached value across finish and streaming prefix checks within the same step.
- Clear the memo when `_check_vocab_boundary_finish` rewrites `output_ids` in place at the same length.
- Preserve the existing decoding path and behavior for all other cases.

## Accuracy Tests

**Passed**: Correctness verification completed.

- All relevant stop-string and speculative decoding unit tests passed.
- Baseline and candidate `finished_reason` and `finished_len` are identical.

title: [Spec] Add --speculative-draft-kv-ratio for all-SWA DFLASH drafts
body:
## Motivation

A DFLASH draft allocates one KV slot per target token, even when every draft layer is sliding-window attention and it can only ever read the last window of what it stores. On Qwen3.8-27B, for example, the draft pool is 8.6 GiB versus the target's 27.5 GiB, which represents a quarter of the KV budget held for rows outside the draft's 2048-token window.

This PR adds a flag to size the draft KV pool as a ratio of the target's capacity for all-SWA DFLASH drafts. On 1xH200 with Qwen3.8-27B and a 5-layer all-SWA draft (draft window 2048, 8 running requests, and 0.8 static memory fraction), a ratio of 0.25 grows the target pool by 21.7%:

| ratio | draft pool | target pool |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 (default) | 450,060 tokens, 8.6 GiB | 450,060 tokens, 27.5 GiB |
| 0.25 | 136,974 tokens, 2.6 GiB | 547,899 tokens, 33.4 GiB (+21.7%) |

## Modifications

- `--speculative-draft-kv-ratio` sizes the draft pool as a fraction of the target's token capacity. At the default of 1.0 nothing changes.
- Below 1.0 the draft's KV becomes the SWA side of the target allocator, which hands out a draft slot with each target slot and owns the full->SWA mapping.
- The radix cache takes its SWA component from the draft's window, so out-of-window draft slots are freed.
- Requires DFLASH. The window defaults to the draft's `sliding_window` unless `--speculative-draft-window-size` is set. Drafts with full-attention layers and targets with sliding-window layers are not supported yet. A ratio too small for the running requests is rejected with the smallest usable value.

## Accuracy Tests

`test/registered/spec/dflash/test_dflash_draft_kv_ratio.py` on 1xH200 with Qwen3.8-27B and the `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` draft. Page size 1 and 64: 9 passed, with GSM8K run once since paging does not affect accuracy. GSM8K 0.98 with accept length 5.75.

`test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_pool_configurator.py` and `test/registered/unit/server_args/test_server_args.py`: 334 passed.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable: this reallocates KV between the target and draft pools and does not touch the compute path.

title: [XPU] Ignore SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE when an XPU is present
body:
SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE=1 turned `import sglang` into an ImportError on a host with a healthy Intel GPU:

  mem_cache/memory_pool.py -> kernels/ops/kvcache/cache_move.py
    ImportError: cannot import name 'copy_all_layer_kv_cache_cpu' from 'sgl_kernel'

The flag selects the CPU engine, which imports `*_cpu` ops from sgl_kernel at module scope, and sgl-kernel-xpu exports none of them -- six modules fail this way in sequence on the entrypoints.engine import path. The flag was also read before any hardware detection, in two independent places, so it overrode a present, working XPU and left get_device() returning "cpu".

Integrations set the flag unconditionally around `import sglang` -- verl's rollout replica loader sets it, imports, then deletes it -- so an XPU host had no way to opt out.

A present XPU now wins over the opt-in in both readers: is_cpu(), which gates every module-scope _is_cpu capture and get_device(), and _is_cpu_available(), which drives platform resolution. The opt-in is logged and ignored, so the variable has no effect at all on an XPU host.

CUDA/ROCm precedence is unchanged: the CUDA wheel does export those symbols, and the opt-in beating CUDA is deliberate and covered by an existing test.

SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE is now registered in Envs so both readers go through the descriptor. This widens accepted values from exactly "1" to the standard EnvBool set (1/true/yes/y).

<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

On a host with a working Intel GPU, `SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE=1` turns a working `import sglang` into an `ImportError`:

```
File ".../sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py", line 45, in <module>
  from sglang.kernels.ops.kvcache.cache_move import (
File ".../sglang/kernels/ops/kvcache/cache_move.py", line 10, in <module>
  from sgl_kernel import copy_all_layer_kv_cache_cpu
ImportError: cannot import name 'copy_all_layer_kv_cache_cpu' from 'sgl_kernel'
```

Two things combine:

1. The flag is read *before* any hardware detection, in two independent places — `utils/common.py::is_cpu` and `platforms/__init__.py::_is_cpu_available` — so it overrides a present, working XPU. `get_device()` then returns `"cpu"`.
2. The CPU engine imports its `*_cpu` ops from `sgl_kernel` at module scope, behind `if _is_cpu:`. Only the CPU wheel (`sglang-kernel-cpu`) exports those names; `sgl-kernel-xpu` exports none of them. Six modules fail this way in sequence on the `entrypoints.engine` import path, each in a module unrelated to the CPU code the caller wanted.

This is a wheel parity gap, not fork drift — the code involved is identical to upstream.

It also is not only an explicit user action. Integrations export the variable unconditionally around `import sglang`: verl's rollout replica loader sets it, imports, then deletes it ([replica.py#L328](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/blob/main/verl/workers/rollout/replica.py#L328)). Because the value is latched at import time, an XPU host had no way to opt out.

Reproduced on `intel/sglang-dev:latest` (1x Intel Arc Pro B60, torch 2.13.0+xpu, sgl_kernel 0.1.8):

```bash
python3 -c "import sglang.srt.entrypoints.engine" && echo B-PASS
SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE=1 python3 -c "import sglang.srt.entrypoints.engine" || echo BUG-REPRODUCED
```

## Modifications

A present XPU now wins over the opt-in, in both readers of the flag:

- **`utils/common.py::is_cpu`** — the kernel-dispatch reader; it gates every module-scope `_is_cpu` capture and `get_device()`. Logs once (`lru_cache`d) and returns `False` when an XPU is present.
- **`platforms/__init__.py::_is_cpu_available`** — platform resolution. Both readers must agree, or kernel dispatch and the resolved platform split for the rest of the process.

CUDA/ROCm precedence is deliberately unchanged: the CUDA wheel does export those symbols, and "opt-in beats CUDA" is documented in `_resolve_platform` and covered by an existing test.

`SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE` is also registered in `Envs`, so both readers go through the descriptor instead of raw `os.getenv`. Note this widens accepted values from exactly `"1"` to the standard `EnvBool` set (`1/true/yes/y`).

Docs updated: `docs/docs/hardware-platforms/xpu.mdx` and `cpu_server.mdx` state that the variable is ignored on XPU hosts.

6 files changed, +65/-5; the source change is 3 files / 18 added lines.

Deliberately out of scope: a CPU-only host running a wheel without the `*_cpu` ops still hits the module-scope `ImportError`. Deferring those imports to their call sites fixes that case too and is a separate, mechanical change if reviewers want it.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable — no kernel or model forward code is touched. The change only decides which engine a process selects. Verified behaviorally on an Arc Pro B60:

| | flag unset | `SGLANG_USE_CPU_ENGINE=1` |
|---|---|---|
| before | `is_cpu=False platform=xpu device=xpu` | `ImportError` at import |
| after | `is_cpu=False platform=xpu device=xpu` | `is_cpu=False platform=xpu device=xpu` + one warning |

The reproducer above now prints `B-PASS` and `A-PASS`.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable, and there is no overhead on the default path: with the flag unset, `is_cpu()` returns after a single env read and never probes `torch.xpu`. The `is_xpu()` call happens only when the flag is set, and `is_cpu()` is `lru_cache`d, so the warning is emitted at most once per process.

Both verified red before the fix and green after; the file's suite passes 75 / 2 skipped.
- [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations) — the two hardware-platform pages above.
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed) — not applicable; see the two sections above for why, and for the behavioral verification used instead.
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

title: [AMD] Restore non-DCP Mamba checkpoint donation to fix agent-mode cache hit at high conc with HiCache
body:
## Motivation

[#39115](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39115) correctly moved Mamba checkpoint depths onto the absolute radix-page grid for DCP, whose allocator pages are wider than scheduler chunk boundaries. Applying the same rule when DCP is disabled suppresses checkpoint donation after chunked prefill leaves an active request off the absolute Mamba chunk grid. For TP2/DCP1 Qwen3.5 AgentX with HiCache at concurrency 20, this nearly doubles computed prompt tokens and reduces the GPU cache hit rate from about 92% to 86%.

Fix: keep #39115’s absolute-page donate mask only when DCP is on; with DCP off, go back to prefix-relative donation (mask = extend_len >= checkpoint_grid) so a chunk that lands off the 64-token grid still donates later chunks.

## Modifications

- Preserve #39115's absolute radix-page checkpoint selection when DCP is enabled.
- Restore prefix-relative Mamba checkpoint donation when DCP is disabled, allowing later chunked-prefill segments to keep donating reusable states.
- Extend the checkpoint-depth unit test to exercise DCP and non-DCP behavior separately, including the observed off-grid active prefix.

## Accuracy Tests

This change does not alter model math or generated outputs. It restores reuse of the same prefix-relative Mamba snapshots used before #39115 for non-DCP serving.

- `test/registered/unit/managers/test_mamba_checkpoint_depth.py`: 7 tests and 4 parameterized DCP cases passed.
- The new non-DCP regression case fails before the fix (`None != 20637`) and passes after it.
- The conc20 validation completed 918 measured requests with zero request errors; 40 warmup requests were excluded from measured results.
- The conc36 validation completed 1,578 measured requests with zero request errors; 74 warmup requests were excluded from measured results.

## Benchmarking and Profiling

Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-MXFP4-AttnFP8-V2, MI355, TP2/DCP1, MTP, HiCache DRAM offload, concurrency 20, 900-second InferenceMax AgentX quick run:

| Build | GPU cache hit | Computed prompt tokens | P90 E2E (ms) | P90 TTFT (ms) | P90 TPOT (ms) | Total throughput (tok/s) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0915 baseline | 92.01% | 7.73M | 13,480 | 1,948 | 7.8 | 72,810 |
| 0922 with #39115 | 86.02% | 14.38M | 21,327 | 3,475 | 10.6 | 68,342 |
| 0922 full #39115 revert | 91.48% | 7.86M | 12,798 | 1,808 | 7.6 | 74,564 |
| 0922 with this fix | 91.42% | 7.89M | 13,696 | 1,915 | 7.4 | 74,397 |

The targeted non-DCP fix matches the full revert's cache reuse and throughput while retaining #39115's DCP page-alignment protection.

Same recipe at concurrency 36 (TP2, KV=dram/HiCache, 1200-second AgentX run; `max-running-requests` capped at 40 so this image does not OOM the Mamba pool at `2*36=72`):

| Build | TP | KV | concurrency | GPU cache hit | Computed prompt tokens | P90 E2E (ms) | total tok/s | total tok/s/gpu | P90 TTFT (ms) | P90 TPOT (ms) |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0922 with #39115 | 2 | dram | 36 | 78.53% | 30.77M | 50,379 | 94,004 | 47,002 | 7,768 | 54.5 |
| 0922 full #39115 revert | 2 | dram | 36 | 88.65% | 16.87M | 27,998 | 124,893 | 62,446 | 4,358 | 20.4 |
| 0922 with this fix | 2 | dram | 36 | 88.48% | 16.79M | 28,676 | 125,506 | 62,753 | 3,783 | 20.9 |

At conc=36 the same off-grid donate miss is larger: GPU hit 78.5% vs 88.5%, computed tokens ~1.8×, P90 E2E 50s vs 29s. This fix again matches the full #39115 revert.

## Why this hits AgentX GPU cache hit (not just Mamba donate counts)

`gpu_cache_hit_rate` is the fraction of prompt tokens served from the device cache instead of recomputed. On a pure attention model, a resident KV page is enough to reuse a prefix. Qwen3.5 is hybrid: a radix node is reusable only if both the KV pages and a Mamba state checkpoint exist at that depth. The Mamba layer is recurrent, so a later request cannot resume from the middle of a sequence without a donated checkpoint.

When the donate mask is false, `req.kv.mamba_last_track_seqlen` stays `None`. `MambaComponent.prepare_for_caching_req` then returns 0 for an unfinished chunk, so that prefill segment is not inserted into the radix tree at all:

```python
if cache_len is None:
    return 0
```

A live conc20 diagnostic (`page=16`, `chunk=64`, `grid=64`) showed the pattern that AgentX actually hits:

```
prefix=0     extend=16384 depth=16384
prefix=16384 extend=16384 depth=32768
prefix=4253  extend=16384 depth=None
prefix=20637 extend=16384 depth=None
prefix=37021 extend=12066 depth=None
```

The first chunk of a request can finish off the absolute 64-token grid (`prefix=4253`). After that, `(aligned - prefix) % 64` is a nonzero constant for every later chunk, so donation never happens again and the rest of a ~90k–100k AgentX prefix never lands in the tree. The next conversation turn theoretically has ~94% prefix reuse, but the server recomputes it.

This is why the regression shows up on AgentX at high concurrency with HiCache, not on short fixed-ISL runs: AgentX median ISL is ~90k–100k tokens with `--chunked-prefill-size 16384`, so one request is six to ten chunks. A single off-grid first chunk poisons every subsequent donation. Short single-chunk prefills start at `prefix=0` and still pass the #39115 mask.

That is the same ~2× computed-token and ~92%→86% GPU-hit gap in the table above.

- [x] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the PR flow. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process).
2. Get approvals from [CODEOWNERS](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/CODEOWNERS) and other reviewers.

title: [DSV4] Fuse native FP8 shared expert into DeepGEMM MegaMoE
body:
## Motivation

Original DeepSeek-V4 checkpoints use MXFP4 routed experts and a blockwise-FP8
shared expert. The existing shared-expert fusion appends the shared expert as a
routed slot, so it cannot preserve this mixed-precision checkpoint contract.

This change uses the native shared-expert inputs added in
`sgl-deep-gemm==0.1.7`. It keeps routed expert count/top-k unchanged and passes
the transformed FP8 shared weights separately to `fp8_fp4_mega_moe`.

Closes #38700.

## Changes

- build separate DeepGEMM L1/L2 layouts from the loaded FP8 shared MLP;
- adapt checkpoint K128 block scales to the native MegaMoE K32 consumer
  contract by repeating each logical value four times before MN-major packing;
- include `num_shared_experts` in the symmetric-buffer shape and cache key,
  alongside upstream's effective DeepGEMM SM budget;
- extend the existing DSV4 pre-dispatch kernel to emit the shared-L1 MN-major
  UE8M0 scale layout during the same activation-quantization pass;
- pass native shared weights to `fp8_fp4_mega_moe` and skip the standalone MLP
  only after those weights have been built;
- apply `routed_scaling_factor` to routed top-k weights before dispatch when
  necessary, so the fused shared result is not scaled accidentally;
- keep W4A4 and all non-MegaMoE paths unchanged.

The path is deliberately restricted to SM100+, DSV4, `fp8xfp4`, one separate
FP8 shared expert, and `[128, 128]` blockwise scales.

## Validation

On NVIDIA B200 with CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.13 + cu130, and
`sgl-deep-gemm==0.1.7`:

- the focused CPU/lifecycle suite passed 23 tests and 9 parameterized subtests;
- the expanded B200 pre-dispatch and real-builder suite passed 9 tests;
- both pre-dispatch JIT specializations compiled on SM100;
- the shared-scale buffer matched an independent DeepGEMM layout for all native
  block-M candidates `{8, 16, 32, 64, 96, 128, 192}`;
- an actual `fp8_fp4_mega_moe` A/B using the fused versus reference scale
  layouts produced exact BF16 equality at `E=8`, `top_k=2`, `H=1024`,
  `I=512`, `tokens=65`;
- the real builder produced the expected DeepSeek-V4-Pro shared scale shapes
  `[6144, 56]` and `[7168, 24]`;
- one-rank CUDA-graph replay matched eager execution exactly, including after
  changing the captured input;
- a same-host NVLink 2xB200 run with uneven local token counts `(65, 71)` passed
  native EP=2 eager-versus-graph and changed-input replay exactness on both
  ranks;
- after rebasing over #39223, the actual SGLang buffer path selected 146 of 148
  SMs for allocation/execution and restored the process-wide setting to 148 on
  both the one- and two-rank runs.

All changed files pass pre-commit after rebasing onto 2026-09-16 `main`.

## Memory and remaining validation

The original shared MLP is retained for batches that exceed the MegaMoE token
cap and fall back to the standalone path. The additional FP8 weight payload is
approximately 1.01 GiB/rank for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 3.75 GiB/rank for
DeepSeek-V4-Pro, before scale/layout padding; the shared MLP is TP1 here.

This PR does not claim full-checkpoint model accuracy or serving throughput.
Those remain explicit follow-up validation gates; the current evidence covers
the scale/layout contract, actual kernel execution, EP=2, and CUDA-graph replay.

title: [AMD][CI] Nightly guard for Qwen3.5-MoE text-only shared-expert fusion loading
body:
## Motivation

[#40754](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40754) fixed `Qwen3_5MoeForCausalLM` (the text-only class `Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B` loads into) silently dropping every `mlp.shared_expert.*` tensor under ROCm aiter shared-expert fusion. The server came up, but the fused MoE slot was never loaded and GSM8K collapsed. No existing nightly runs that code:

- The Qwen3.5 AMD nightlies (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`) load the multimodal `Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`, which already had the remap.
- The Qwen3.8 MXFP4 MI35x nightly loads `Qwen3_5MoeForCausalLM`, but its Quark checkpoint keeps the shared expert in BF16, so `QuarkConfig.can_fuse_shared_expert()` turns fusion off.
- Qwen3.8 FP8 (~2.5 TB) needs two nodes (#40754 was verified at TP8 x PP2 on 2x MI300X), and AMD nightly jobs are single-node.

## Modifications

New `test/registered/amd/test_qwen35_moe_text_shared_expert_fusion.py` in the `nightly-amd-1-gpu` suite. The existing `nightly-test-1-gpu-unit` job (MI300, 1 GPU) already runs that suite, so there are no workflow changes.

The test builds a seeded 4-layer random-weight `Qwen3_5MoeForCausalLM` checkpoint (~1.1 GiB) with Qwen3.8's config keys, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's layer widths, and 32 experts with top-8. It serves the checkpoint with `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1` and compares prompt logprobs against the same weights served with `--disable-shared-experts-fusion`:

- **Stacked 3-D experts** (the Qwen3.8 BF16 layout): the fused server must match the unfused one.
- **One tensor per expert** (the Qwen3.8 FP8 layout, minus scales): the fused server must match too. The loader maps the shared expert on a separate branch for each layout.
- **Negative control:** a copy with the shared expert zeroed must move the logprobs far past the pass bound.
- **Path check:** every launch verifies it really ran fused or unfused as requested (`/server_info` plus the Qwen3.5 gate's auto-disable log), so neither side can quietly fall back.

## Accuracy Tests

AMD hardware validation is in progress: [Nightly Test (AMD) run #36080103606](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36080103606) targets `nightly-test-1-gpu-unit` on ROCm 10 / MI300 at commit `96b2582`. The test has not completed. CPU checks:

- **Checkpoint format:** it loads cleanly into transformers 5.12.1 `Qwen3_5MoeForCausalLM`, its tensor names match both Qwen3.8 checkpoints exactly, and sglang's `get_config` parses it as `Qwen3_5MoeTextConfig`.
- **Loader:** sglang's real `load_weights` with fusion on, against stub params that record every load:

  | Code | Shared expert in fused slot | `shared_expert ... not found in params_dict` |
  |---|---|---|
  | main | loaded exactly, both layouts | 0 |
  | #40754 reverted | never loaded, both layouts | 12 per layout |

- **Thresholds:** mean |logprob difference| per prompt token, measured with the transformers reference:
  - simulated fused-vs-unfused BF16 drift: 0.011–0.018
  - BF16 vs FP32: 0.024
  - shared expert zeroed: 0.98

  So the pass bound is 0.1, and the negative control must exceed 0.5.
- **Dry run:** the real test class, run against a fake server backed by the reference model, passes when fusion is correct. It fails when the shared expert is dropped, when fusion is silently disabled, or when the reference ignores the disable flag.



## Speed Tests and Profiling

N/A (test only). It takes about 10 minutes of one MI300 per ROCm image (`est_time=600`, well inside the 900 s per-file timeout). Checkpoints go to a temp dir, not the shared `/sgl-data` cache.

title: [AMD] [GLM5] Add opt-in PTPC FP8 projections on gfx950
body:
## Motivation

The `amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4` checkpoint keeps the q_a, kv_a, q_b, and o attention projections in BF16. They are represented by three modules: `fused_qkv_a_proj_with_mqa`, `q_b_proj`, and `o_proj`.

This PR adds a default-off PTPC FP8 path on gfx950 using per-token activation scales and per-channel weight scales. BF16 remains the default and fallback.

## Modifications

- Add `SGLANG_DSA_FP8_PROJ_GEMM` as the single opt-in switch; the path also requires Aiter, gfx950, and the GLM DSA model type.
- Cache bpreshuffled FP8 weights while retaining the original BF16 parameters for fallback, so enabled projections hold both copies.
- Fold q_b input quantization into the existing q/k RMSNorm in the active ROCm MHA/MLA forward paths. o_proj uses a standalone per-token quantization of the ROCm MLA attention output.
- Keep `fused_qkv_a_proj_with_mqa` on tuned Aiter BF16 for M≤512 and use PTPC FP8 for M>512; the threshold was selected empirically on MI355X. q_b_proj and o_proj use FP8 whenever the flag is enabled.
- Fall back to Triton quantization helpers on Aiter builds without the HIP fused per-token RMSNorm kernel.

title: [Metrics] Add request-level TPOT histogram (sglang:request_time_per_output_token_seconds)
body:
Related metrics PRs: #38600, #39706. Each is independent and they can merge in any order.

## Motivation

SGLang exports token-weighted inter-token latency but no request-weighted time per output token (TPOT). This adds `sglang:request_time_per_output_token_seconds`, observed once per qualifying request:

```text
TPOT = (finished_time - first_token_time) / (completion_tokens - 1)
```

Non-streaming TPOT is only accurate once #38600 lands: without it, non-streaming `first_token_time` is stamped late. Streaming TPOT is unaffected. The code does not depend on #38600 or #39706.

## Modifications

- Record TPOT for requests that finish with `stop` or `length`, have more than one output token, and have an observed decode interval. Skip aborts and PD prefill workers.
- When the first output is also the final one, stamp both times with the same timestamp so no false decode interval appears.
- Reuse `--bucket-inter-token-latency` buckets and label by `is_streaming`.
- `meta_info["decode_throughput"]` uses the same calculation (`APIServerReqTimeStats.get_time_per_output_token`).
- Docs: describe the metric and delete the stale `sglang:time_per_output_token_seconds` sample block. That metric is no longer emitted.

## Tests

- `test_req_time_stats.py`: formula and undefined cases (2 methods).
- `test_stat_loggers_di.py`: observation with the `is_streaming` label, and no observation when undefined (2 methods).
- `test_tokenizer_manager_rid_cleanup.py::TestRequestTpotGating`, through the real `_handle_batch_output` (2 methods): a single-batch finish records nothing; across two batches, `stop` records one value while abort and PD prefill record nothing. Each of these mutations fails a test: dropping `ts=first_output_time`, making the stop/length filter always true, or making the prefill check always true.
- `test/registered/observability/test_metrics.py` (GPU e2e): checks that `sglang:request_time_per_output_token_seconds_count{is_streaming="true"}` is positive.

CPU: this PR's unit files pass on `main` (107 tests), and together with #38600 and #39706 in any merge order (115 tests).

title: fix: propagate weight checker failures across TP ranks
body:
## Motivation

With TP=2, `/weights_checker` can return HTTP 200 and `success: true` after a snapshot even when a weight changed only on TP1. TP1 logs the mismatch, but the egress rank answers before seeing it. `compare` has no checksum payload, so the existing code skips the TP gather that runs for `checksum`.

## Modifications

- Gather each rank's local error and optional checksum payload for every weight-check action. Any TP-rank failure now returns a rank-labeled failure through the HTTP API.
- Keep the existing one-`ChecksumInfo`-per-TP-rank checksum response. A local checksum exception also joins the collective, so its peers do not wait there until timeout.
- Add registered CPU regression tests for a nonzero-rank compare failure, a checksum exception on one rank, and the checksum payload shape.

## Validation

- Before the fix, a real two-H200 TP=2/DP=1/PP=1 HTTP reproduction on unmodified main (`6bbd689a`) returned 200 for unchanged weights, 400 for TP0-only corruption, and **200** for TP1-only corruption while TP1 logged the mismatch.
- With this patch on main `8ca82118`, the same three public-API cases returned **200, 400, 400**. The TP1-only failure response names `TP rank 1` and the mismatched parameter.
- Registered CPU unit test: 3 passed in the SGLang-capable GPU image. `pre-commit run --files` for both changed files, `py_compile`, and `git diff --check` passed.

This changes only the admin weight-check path; model outputs and inference performance are unaffected. The live test covers TP=2/DP=1/PP=1. Related work: #26863 added multi-GPU checksum gathering; #35093 concerns rank-local tensor-update failures.

## Checklist

- [x] Format the changed files with pre-commit.
- [x] Add focused registered unit tests.
- [x] Verify the HTTP behavior on a real two-GPU server.

title: Let predicate-registered linear-attention models carry the mamba radix-cache leaves
body:
## Motivation

- A hybrid linear-attention model can register either by architecture name or by a predicate on its HF config.
- The mamba radix-cache resolution and the validation from #37474 only looked the spec up by architecture name, and extra-buffer support came only from a hard-coded set of architectures.
- A predicate-registered model therefore never got its mamba radix-cache leaf: auto could not pick the extra-buffer strategy, and an explicit extra-buffer strategy was rejected as "needs mamba state". Out-of-tree models had to patch the architecture sets, even though the spec already carries the information, including an unused extra-buffer support field.

## Modifications

- (-) Spec lookup by architecture name only, extra-buffer support from the hard-coded set only, and the resolution, validation, and hook helpers took an architecture string.
- (+) One lookup resolves the spec by architecture name first and by config predicate second, the spec's extra-buffer field is honoured under the same triton-backend condition, and the helpers take the HF config so the name and the spec come from one input. Behaviour for hard-coded and arch-registered models is unchanged; unit tests cover predicate-registered specs (auto and explicit), predicate misses, and arch-registered specs without the opt-in.

Possible follow-up: migrate the hard-coded architecture sets onto registry specs so the registry becomes the single source of truth.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable: server-argument resolution only.

title: [DeepEP v2] Let a model package supply its per-rank prefill dispatch bound
body:
## Motivation

`validate_deepep_v2_dispatch_token_budget` compares the whole prefill-buffer ceiling (`--chunked-prefill-size` / `--max-prefill-tokens`) against `SGLANG_DEEPEP_V2_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK`. A model package that scatters each prefill chunk over its attention-TP group before the MoE dispatch (sequence-parallel prefill under DP attention) sends only a fraction of that ceiling from any one rank, so the unsharded check rejects configurations that fit. For example, a 32768-token per-DP ceiling scattered over 8 attention-TP ranks dispatches 4096 tokens per rank.

The DeepEP v2 registry already lets an external model package declare its architecture and its MXFP8 precision policy. This extends that same entry point so the package can also declare how its prefill dispatch is sized, without SGLang core learning anything model-specific.

## Modifications

- `python/sglang/srt/configs/moe_model_registry.py`: the registry value becomes a frozen `msgspec.Struct` policy holding `silu_mul_keep_fp32` and an optional `prefill_dispatch_tokens` callback. `register_deepep_v2_model` accepts `prefill_dispatch_tokens(cfg, tokens)`, which receives the resolved read-only configuration and the prefill-buffer ceiling and returns the maximum tokens one rank dispatches. Re-registering an architecture with a different policy still raises. `model_deepep_v2_prefill_dispatch_tokens(hf_config, cfg, default_tokens)` applies the primary architecture's callback, or returns the ceiling unchanged when none is registered. The built-in architectures keep the default policy, so their behavior does not change.
- `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/moe_hook.py`: `required_deepep_v2_prefill_tokens_per_rank` sizes the prefill budget through the registry, and the prefill branch of `validate_deepep_v2_dispatch_token_budget` uses it. Scheduler and buffer settings and the decode-graph budget check are unchanged.
- `test/registered/unit/layers/moe/test_hpc_ops_runner_guard.py`: the registration test now covers the callback applied on the primary architecture, the unchanged ceiling when the primary architecture is unregistered, and the conflict raised when an architecture is re-registered with the same precision flag but a different callback.

The policy container is a `msgspec.Struct` rather than a dataclass, following `.claude/rules/no-dataclasses.md`.

## Original commits

- `3f86c79b66e`

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable: this changes server-argument validation only, not any kernel or forward path.

title: [Feature] Extend set_internal_state to hot scheduler knobs
body:
## Motivation

`set_internal_state` already fans out to every scheduler rank, but its allowlist admits only five niche keys. The settings operators actually tune, concurrency cap, queue limit, prefill chunk size, prefill budget, schedule policy, are read by the event loop on every step and are plain Python state, yet changing one means killing the server and reloading the weights. On the machines below that is one to seven minutes per change.

This widens the existing route to those knobs. No new endpoint, no new transport, no kernels, no architecture-specific code.

| knob | accepted values | where the loop reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `max_running_requests` | 1 to the boot allocation | scheduler.py 2274, 2302, 3626 |
| `max_queued_requests` | 0 or more | scheduler.py 3077 |
| `chunked_prefill_size` | above 0 | scheduler.py 3600 |
| `max_prefill_tokens` | 1 to `max_total_num_tokens` | scheduler.py 3621 |
| `schedule_policy` | any `SchedulePolicy`, via `_validate_and_adjust_policy` | schedule_policy.py 257, 294, 297 |
| `schedule_conservativeness` | above 0, rebuilds the watermarks as `from_config` does | scheduler.py 3620, 3890 |
| `log_level` | DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR | every log call |

`get_internal_state` reports the live values and the boot ceilings under a `trimtab` key. `SetInternalStateReq.server_args` widens to allow `str` for the two string knobs. Unknown keys fall through to the existing allowlist untouched, so the five upstream keys behave exactly as before.

## Modifications

- `python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py`: `_trimtab_apply_hot_knobs` applies and validates the knobs, called at the top of `set_internal_state`; `get_internal_state` reports them.
- `python/sglang/srt/managers/io_struct.py`: `server_args` accepts `str` values.
- `test/registered/unit/managers/test_trimtab_hot_knobs.py`: new, CPU only.

The in-place KV pool reinit that was in the first version of this PR has been split out. It is the risky half, it deserves its own review, and it will follow once this lands.

## Accuracy Test

No model behaviour changes. These are scheduler admission and batching settings; the sampling path is untouched.

## Benchmark and Profiling

Measured on H100, RTX PRO 6000 and B200 with Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 under 32-thread load: 20 of 20 changes applied, p50 16 to 22 ms round trip, zero failed requests across every run. The same settings changed by restart cost 56 to 86 s warm and 141 to 391 s cold on the same machines.

## Checklist

- [x] Format the code with `pre-commit run --all-files` (ruff, ruff-format and isort clean over the touched files; the diff against main is additive only)
- [x] Add unit tests under `test/registered/unit/`
- [x] Measured on real hardware, numbers above

Parts of this change and its tests were written with AI assistance; every line has been reviewed and the behaviour verified on the hardware listed.

title: [ROCm][Bugfix] Keep quantization for mixed Quark Qwen3.5 MTP checkpoints
body:
## Motivation

Speculative decoding is currently not working for amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4 (NEXTN, TP8, gfx950), because MTP does not load on mixed Quark MXFP4 Qwen3.5 checkpoints. This PR fixes the issue by addressing two separate problems:

`_mtp_quant_config` drops the draft's quant config as soon as any `mtp.*` layer appears in the Quark exclude list. That is correct for checkpoints whose MTP module is entirely bf16 (#23146), but here it builds the whole draft unquantized, so the MoE loader allocates bf16 experts that the MXFP4 checkpoint shards no longer fit.

`Qwen3_5ForCausalLMMTP` declares no `packed_modules_mapping`, which the loader reads off the model class so the quant config can expand `qkv_proj` into `q_proj`/`k_proj`/`v_proj` before matching the exclude list. Without it an excluded attention projection is allocated MXFP4 - half as wide once packed - against bf16 shards.

## Modifications

Two changes in `python/sglang/srt/models/qwen3_5_mtp.py`:

- `_mtp_quant_config`: the Quark branch now takes the whole-module skip only when the routed experts are excluded as well, rather than on any `mtp.*` entry. They are the bulk of the draft, and the ordinary per-layer exclusions keep attention, the shared expert and `fc` in bf16 on their own.
- `Qwen3_5ForCausalLMMTP`: declare `packed_modules_mapping`, aliasing the target model's as `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration` already does. That is also what the `TODO` above the Quark block in `_get_quantization_config` asks for.

`test/registered/unit/models/test_qwen3_5_mtp_quant_config.py` is new, covered under Accuracy Tests below.

Nothing else changes behaviour. The `mtp.*` exclude lists of the two published AMD checkpoints are identical apart from the routed experts:

| checkpoint | `mtp.*` excludes | of which `mlp.experts` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| amd/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-MXFP4 | 1546 | 1536 (= 512 x 3) |
| amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4 | 10 | 0 |

So the 397B still takes the skip and is unaffected. The only lists whose behaviour changes are Quark lists naming some `mtp.*` layers but not the routed experts, which is exactly the mixed case.

One side effect worth flagging: `_get_quantization_config` mutates the mapping it reads off the class, so a Quark run now adds `fused_qkv_a_proj_with_mqa` to `Qwen3_5ForCausalLM.packed_modules_mapping` process-wide. It is harmless here and `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration` already aliases the same dict, but I can copy instead if you prefer.

## Accuracy Tests

The draft loads and serves on `amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4`, NEXTN 3/1/4, TP8, MI350X; without this change it fails at load. New CPU-only unit tests cover both checkpoint shapes, using the real exclude entries, including a regression guard for #23146.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

None; this only changes which weights are allocated quantized at load time.

title: [Feature] Support Lark grammars with XGrammar
body:
## Motivation

XGrammar 0.2.7 provides `GrammarCompiler.compile_lark`, but SGLang currently sends the existing `ebnf` grammar input only to `compile_grammar`. As a result, XGrammar cannot accept Lark syntax through the established grammar API.

## Modifications

- Pin XGrammar to the stable 0.2.7 release.
- Keep the existing `ebnf` sampling parameter and public API unchanged.
- In the XGrammar backend, compile as EBNF first and fall back to `compile_lark` when EBNF parsing fails.
- Preserve the resolved grammar format in compilation statistics and report both parser errors when neither format is valid.
- Document that XGrammar accepts Lark syntax through the existing `ebnf` parameter.
- Add focused XGrammar unit coverage for EBNF compilation, Lark fallback, real compilation with XGrammar 0.2.7, and invalid input.

## Accuracy Tests

Focused Python unit tests:

    159 passed, 36 subtests passed

The tests include real compilation of both `root ::= "yes" | "no"` and `start: "yes" | "no"` through `XGrammarGrammarBackend.dispatch_ebnf` with XGrammar 0.2.7.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable. Existing valid EBNF inputs retain the same compilation and decoding path. Lark compilation occurs only after the EBNF parser rejects the input.

title: [Sampling] Stream sampling masks as per-request arrays
body:
## Motivation

`return_sampling_mask` returns, for every output token, the support the sampler drew from and its behavior logprob(s). That is `L` token IDs per token, plus `L` logprobs in `support` mode. `L` is the realized support size: tens under a typical `top_p`, up to `top_k` otherwise.

On `main` the support crosses the whole output path as Python objects:

- **Scheduler:** every step does a torch slice plus `.tolist()` per request row, and each `Req` keeps its full support history until it finishes.
- **IPC:** the scheduler pickles nested lists; the detokenizer unpickles and re-pickles them; the tokenizer manager unpickles them again.

At 256 concurrent requests with ~1000-token supports in `support` mode, that costs `main`'s scheduler ~28 ms of row bookkeeping per decode step. It also stalls ~0.43 s on every 50-token emission, or 3.7 s at `top_k=8192`. A decode step is ~14 ms, so overlap scheduling cannot hide this, and under DP attention the slowest rank gates every rank.

## Contract

- **Response:** byte-identical to `main` (see Correctness). `output_token_sampling_mask`, `output_token_sampling_logprobs`, `output_token_sampling_mask_length` and streaming slices come from the same float32 → Python float conversions.
- **Sampling:** the sampler, including mask capture and packing, is untouched.
- **No opt-in, no cost:** when no request asks for masks, no work, allocation or IPC payload is added.

## Design

Treat the support as bulk numeric data from the sampler to the tokenizer manager, and create Python objects only where the response format requires them, once.

1. **Scheduler** (commit 1).
   - Each committed token copies its row, taken from numpy views of the step's host buffers, into the request's `SamplingMaskRows`.
   - The queue buffers double in capacity, so each byte is copied O(1) times regardless of the allocator.
   - On emission `take()` hands the rows off as a `SamplingMaskChunk` of int32/float32 arrays without copying. The handed-off buffer becomes a spare that is reused only once no view of it remains (checked by refcount), so steady-state appends write to warm pages.
2. **IPC** (commit 1). `output_token_sampling_mask` becomes `Optional[List[Optional[SamplingMaskChunk]]]`: one chunk per request. This follows the existing per-request buffer fields (`decode_ids: List[array]`, `input_top_logprobs_*_flat: List[np.ndarray]`), so the detokenizer passes it through and multi-tokenizer routing uses the generic `_extract_field_by_index` unchanged.
3. **Tokenizer manager** (commit 1). `SamplingMaskChunk.to_lists()` builds the response lists.
4. **GC-neutral chunk pickling** (commits 4 and 5).
   - numpy's own array reducer, and wrapping a `bytearray` with `np.frombuffer` (whose base becomes a GC-tracked `memoryview`), each leave GC-tracked objects per array. When every message carries one short chunk per request, as with per-token streaming, those objects doubled the tokenizer manager's young-generation collections. That promoted its accumulated lists into 3.5× more full collections than on `main`.
   - A chunk therefore pickles its three buffers as read-only `bytes` and rebuilds them with `np.frombuffer`. The bytes are unchanged, unpickling leaves no tracked objects, and protocols below 5 keep the default reduction.
5. **Zero-copy send** (commit 2). `sock_send` / `async_sock_send` pass `copy=False` to zmq.
   - pyzmq's default copies every encoded message into a new zmq buffer before returning. With `copy=False`, zmq sends the freshly encoded bytes in place; they are never mutated or shared.
   - pyzmq still copies messages below `Socket.copy_threshold` (64 KiB), so small messages take the identical path.
   - The wire bytes, and therefore every receiver, are unchanged.
   - Sender-side cost with a live receiver: below 64 KiB unchanged; 1 MiB 110 → 26 µs; 16 MiB 1.5 ms → 45 µs; 840 MiB 225 ms → 85 µs.

### Checks removed, and why they are safe

Each removed check guarded a state that `main` already rules out before the check runs. Links point to `main`.

1. **Length re-validation in `materialize_sampling_mask_output`** ([`if status == OK and not (0 <= length <= packed_width)`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py#L1207)).
   - The sampler emits [`lengths = realized_lengths.clamp(max=packed_size)`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py#L587).
   - Its packed IDs have exactly `packed_size` columns: [top-k](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py#L570), [PyTorch producer](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py#L575), and [greedy, width 1 with length 1](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py#L475-L476).
   - So `0 <= length <= packed_width` always holds.
2. **`None` rows in `add_sampling_mask_return_values`** ([`None if mask is None else mask[i]`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py#L1168)). Every caller appends only after `get_sampling_mask_finish_reason` returned no abort, which means the status was OK:
   - [decode](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py#L1007-L1039);
   - [non-PD prefill](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py#L402-L406);
   - [PD prefill](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L845-L916).

   A missing capture has status `None` and is [aborted as well](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/batch_result_processor.py#L1242). An OK status always materializes its row.
3. **PD prefill `set_buf`**: the `-1` sentinel, the empty-queue and `None`-row branches, and the capacity `RuntimeError` ([`utils.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/utils.py#L515-L560)).
   - **The first row is queued:** it is [appended](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L916) right before the [last-chunk send](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L920), or before the [send after a pending bootstrap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L1042). `set_buf` runs [only on the last chunk](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L1378). Prefill streams a request only on abort ([L438](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L438), [L983](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L983), [L1198](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L1198)), after which nothing is sent, or [after its KV transfer](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L1092).
   - **The row is not `None`:** same status guarantee as 2.
   - **The row fits the buffer:** the prefill buffer's width is [`--sampling-mask-max-tokens`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1514), the same cap the sampler uses. A longer support gets [OVERFLOW status](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py#L542) and is aborted by 2.
4. **PD decode `if sampling_mask_len < 0`** ([`decode.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/81f2b43ab512cbc1e2ca0aef97b93e224d400a69/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/decode.py#L2546)). It only matched the `-1` sentinel, which prefill can no longer write; per 3, `main` never reached it either. The length the decode side reads is the one the prefill wrote for the same request, which is at least 1.

Nothing enforces that prefill and decode use the same `--sampling-mask-max-tokens`; the flag's help text asks for it. That holds on `main` too, and none of the removed checks guarded it.

The per-request queue relies on one more property: a chunk is serialized before its request's next append. `sock_send` encodes synchronously, and the stream accumulator is local to `stream_output`. The refcount check keeps buffer recycling safe even if a chunk were retained.

### Alternatives measured and rejected

- **One CSR payload per batch** concatenates every request's rows before pickling. Pickle already writes each request's buffer into its stream, so the concat was a pure extra copy. It measured 4× slower to encode than per-request arrays at 210 MB.
- **`array.array` queues** (the `Req.output_ids` primitive) over-allocate by 1/16, so appending 32 KB rows reallocates nearly every step. Once glibc's dynamic mmap threshold has risen, that realloc copies the whole buffer. It was 48% of live scheduler time at `top_k=8192`. A microbenchmark that appended into fresh buffers missed it.
- **FlashInfer radix `top_k` for packing** matches `torch.topk`'s (id, logprob) pairs, lengths and statuses on identical captures. However, with bf16 logits it orders tied token IDs differently in nearly every row, so responses would no longer be byte-identical to `main`. It saved ~0.3 ms of GPU time per step at batch 256.
- **An R3-style preallocated pool indexed by KV slot** is how routed experts are gathered. It fits fixed-width rows, but sampling-mask rows are up to `--sampling-mask-max-tokens` wide: for example, 500k slots × 4096 × 8 B = 16 GB.

### Internal signature changes

| Where | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `BatchTokenIDOutput` / `BatchStrOutput` | two nested-list fields | `output_token_sampling_mask: Optional[List[Optional[SamplingMaskChunk]]]` (`output_token_sampling_logprobs` removed) |
| `Req` | `output_token_sampling_mask`, `output_token_sampling_logprobs`, `send_output_sampling_mask_offset` | `sampling_mask_rows: Optional[SamplingMaskRows]` |
| `LogitsProcessorOutput.next_token_sampling_mask_idx` / `_logprobs` | Python lists | numpy row views |

## Performance

All end-to-end numbers are same-host A/B: one Modal H100 container launches the server from `main` and then from this branch.

- **Setup:** Qwen3-8B, `temperature=1`, `ignore_eos`, default overlap scheduler and pickle IPC; non-streaming unless noted.
- **Metric:** steady-state decode throughput (tok/s), from the scheduler's decode log over windows where every request is running.

**TP1, 512 new tokens**

| batch | `top_k` / `top_p` (mean support) | mask off | selected: main → PR | support: main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 1000 / 1.0 (~1011) | 18427 → 18415 | 10444 → **16274** (+56%) | 5426 → **16236** (+199%) |
| 64 | 1000 / 1.0 (~1011) | 7529 → 7529 | 6060 → **7053** (+16%) | 4569 → **7035** (+54%) |
| 256 | 1024 / 0.95 (~10) | 18551 → 18483 | 15896 → 15888 (0%) | 15453 → 15866 (+3%) |
| 256 | 20 / 1.0 (20) | 18528 → 18525 | 16577 → 16594 (0%) | 15947 → 16537 (+4%) |
| 1 | any | 150 → 150 | 145 → 145 | 145 → 144 |

**DP attention** (`--tp 2 --dp 2 --enable-dp-attention`, 256 requests per rank, per-rank throughput)

| `top_k` / `top_p` | mask off | selected: main → PR | support: main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 / 1.0 | 16836 → 16879 | 7940 → **15032** (+89%) | 3943 → **14506** (+268%) |
| 1024 / 0.95 | 16775 → 16915 | 14697 → 14799 (+1%) | 13169 → 14642 (+11%) |

In support mode the sampling return now costs 2.5 ms per decode step against a 15.2 ms step.

**`top_k=8192`, batch 256** (256 new tokens, `--sampling-mask-max-tokens 9216`; mask off is 20961 → 20985)

| mode | decode tok/s: main → PR | wall s: main → PR | wall with `--tokenizer-worker-num 8`: main → PR | scheduler RSS GB: main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| selected | 1640 → **14797** (9.0×) | 63.5 → 36.0 | 63.6 → 37.0 | 29.9 → 8.9 |
| support | 811 → **12590** (15.5×) | 151.5 → 88.4 | 150.0 → 83.3 | 52.1 → 9.5 |

Even here, support mode adds 8.1 ms per decode step against a 12.2 ms step.

**RL rollouts with staggered finishes.** Batch 256, `ignore_eos`. Each request's `max_new_tokens` is spread evenly over the listed range, so requests finish at different steps. The metric is wall time for the whole batch. Mask off is the same requests without `return_sampling_mask`, which has no mode.

| `top_k` | output tokens | mask off | selected: main → PR | support: main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 64–1024 | 11.5 s | 12.8 → 12.5 s | 14.0 → **12.5 s** |
| 256 | 64–1024 | 11.5 s | 13.5 → 12.5 s | 15.5 → **12.5 s** |
| 8192 | 64–1024 | 11.2 s | 85.8 → **62.5 s** | not run |
| 8192 | 32–512 | 5.2 s | not run | 124.7 → **88.6 s** |

At `top_k` 128–256, the sampling return adds about 1 s to an 11.5 s rollout. At `top_k=8192`, the tokenizer manager's list building bounds wall time (see Limitations). The support run uses half the output tokens to bound its response size. Scheduler RSS drops from 24.8 to 8.8 GB (selected) and from 23.0 to 9.3 GB (support).

**Commit 2 alone** (same-container A/B of this branch without → with it)

| workload | selected | support |
|---|---|---|
| TP1, batch 256, `top_k=8192` | 13114 → 15291 (+17%) | 10022 → 12808 (+28%) |
| TP1, batch 256, `top_k=1000` | 15912 → 16301 (+2%) | 15225 → 16120 (+6%) |
| DP attention, 256/rank, `top_k=1000` | 14630 → 15055 (+3%) | 13761 → 14391 (+5%) |

With mask off or supports of at most 20 tokens, results stay within ±0.5%. At `top_k=8192` in support mode, the sampling return adds 13.5 ms per decode step without this commit and 7.9 ms with it, against a 12.1 ms step.

**Streaming** (`stream_interval=1`, `--incremental-streaming-output`, batch 256; mask off 20419)

| `top_k` | selected: main → PR | support: main → PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 7696 → **18328** | 3937 → **18100** |
| 20 | 18477 → 18541 | 16639 → 18313 |

End-to-end wall time for streaming is at or below `main` in every configuration of this suite, in both run orders. At `top_k=1000` × 256 it goes 24.0 → 19.0 s in support mode and 12.8 → 10.0 s in selected mode.

**Per stage, batch 256, support mode.** This is a same-container microbenchmark of the same code on an H100 host. An "emission" is one 50-token chunk.

| stage | `top_k=1000`: main → PR | `top_k=8192`: main → PR |
|---|---|---|
| scheduler row bookkeeping per step | 31.8 → 0.89 ms | 239 → 3.0 ms |
| scheduler per emission (pickle + send) | 532 → 115 ms | 4.46 → 1.10 s |
| detokenizer per emission (unpickle + re-pickle) | 1.84 s → 89 ms | 14.8 → 1.27 s |
| tokenizer manager per emission (unpickle + build lists) | 1.39 → 1.48 s | 10.8 → 13.1 s |
| GPU capture and packing per step (unchanged) | 1.98 → 1.97 ms | 2.18 → 2.18 ms |

**Profiler.** A same-host torch profiler capture of 40 steady decode steps (batch 256, `top_k=1000`):

| mode | GPU busy: main → PR | time per step: main → PR | longest `process_batch_result`: main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| mask off | 96% → 96% | 13.8 → 13.9 ms | 21 → 21 ms |
| selected | 31% → **96%** | 44.2 → 14.9 ms | 513 → 12 ms |
| support | 22% → **96%** | 57.0 → 15.9 ms | 447 → 14 ms |

## Correctness

The optimization must not change what clients receive in either mode. Two tests in this PR (commit 3) pin that contract:

- **CPU, `test_clients_receive_the_sampler_rows_unchanged`:** drives sampler-shaped outputs through materialization, the per-request queues, stream emissions at arbitrary steps and both IPC codecs. Every request's lists must equal the direct conversion of the sampler's rows: `token_ids[row, :length]` with `selected_logprobs[row]` or `support_logprobs[row, :length]`.
- **GPU, `test_modes_and_streaming_return_identical_sampling_masks`** (deterministic inference): for the same seeded tokens, selected and support mode must return the same supports, and each selected logprob must equal the sampled token's support logprob. A per-token stream must match the response emitted every 50 tokens.

Both tests fail against a deliberately broken transport (queued lengths not cleared on hand-off), while the pre-existing suite still passes on it.

Separately, a fixed workload of 54 requests is sent to `main` twice (a reproducibility control), then to this branch, in the same container, and the responses are diffed exactly (floats compared bitwise). The fields compared are `text`, `output_ids`, `finish_reason`, `completion_tokens`, the three sampling-mask fields and `output_token_logprobs`.

The workload covers:

- selected, support and mask-off requests in one batch;
- `top_k` from 1 to 1000, `top_p` and temperature variants;
- natural and `ignore_eos` stops, and 120 tokens so every request crosses the 50-token forced emission;
- non-streaming and streaming requests;
- `return_logprob` together with masks.

All runs use `--enable-deterministic-inference` (PyTorch sampler, per-request seeds).

| configuration | main vs main | main vs PR |
|---|---|---|
| requests sent one at a time | 54/54 identical | **54/54 identical** |
| concurrent requests | 54/54 identical | 51/54 identical¹ |
| concurrent, msgpack IPC (`SGLANG_USE_PICKLE_IPC=false`) | 54/54 identical | **54/54 identical** |
| concurrent, `--tokenizer-worker-num 2` | 53/54 identical¹ | 52/54 identical¹ |
| concurrent, `--incremental-streaming-output` | 54/54 identical | **54/54 identical** |

¹ Every difference, including the one between two runs of `main`, is in the logprobs of row 0: the token sampled at prefill, 1–4 float32 ulps apart. Its support IDs, `text` and `output_ids` are identical. It depends on how concurrent requests share prefill batches, and it disappears when requests are sent one at a time. The transport copies float32 bits without arithmetic, and the CPU test above checks that bit for bit.

Each configuration covers 4320 mask rows. The default FlashInfer sampler is not reproducible run to run: `main` itself differs from `main` in float32 last bits (max 1.9e-6) of a few rows, with identical support sets. Under it, this branch gives identical `text`/`output_ids` and differs only within that same noise.

## Limitations

- **The response format itself costs Python objects.** The tokenizer manager builds one int per support entry, plus one float in support mode. At `top_k=8192` × 256 this is ~10 s of tokenizer CPU per 50-token cycle, and it bounds wall time. In the staggered `top_k=8192` rollouts above, it accounts for most of the gap to mask-off: 62.5 s against 11.2 s in selected mode.
  - It runs off the scheduler and scales with `--tokenizer-worker-num`.
  - About a quarter of it is cyclic GC walking the freshly built lists. The existing `--gc-threshold 100000` cut tokenizer GC time from 2.4 to 0.5 s and wall time by 9% on a 256 × 256-token `top_k=1000` support run.
  - Removing the cost entirely would need an opt-in binary response format.
- **Emissions still copy once into the pickle stream.** Non-streaming requests emit every 50 tokens in the same step, and pickling copies each chunk into freshly allocated memory. At `top_k=8192` × 256 in support mode, that is about 5 ms per decode step amortized. Pickle protocol 5's out-of-band buffers, sent as extra zmq frames, would remove this copy on every hop. It is an IPC-wide change (received numpy arrays become read-only views of zmq frames), so it belongs in its own PR.
- **D2H is sized by capacity, not by the realized support.** The packed `[B, --sampling-mask-max-tokens]` buffer crosses every step; it overlaps on the copy stream.
- **Capture keeps its two full-vocabulary renorm kernels,** at 2.0 ms per step against 0.36 ms for sampling alone at batch 256. A fused capture kernel would be a follow-up.

## Testing

- **CPU unit tests:** `test/registered/unit/{managers,disaggregation,sampling}` plus the OpenAI protocol and serving-chat tests.
  - 1619 passed with 970 subtests; `main` passes 1617 in the same run.
  - Both trees share the same pre-existing failure, `test_mm_process_config` (cross-test state; it passes alone), and two collection errors from the CPU image (`parameterized` missing, no accelerator).
- **New streamer case:** queued rows cross both the pickle and msgpack codecs once, in batch order, and expand to the response lists. It also checks that rows queued later never overwrite a chunk that is still referenced; the case fails with the refcount check removed.
- **GPU:** `test/registered/sampling/test_sampling_mask.py` on 2×H100: 35 passed with 28 subtests, covering FlashInfer and PyTorch sampling, deterministic inference, TP=2 and PP=2.
- **Benchmark validation:** every benchmark response checks three things:
  - the mask count equals the output length;
  - the sampled token is in its support;
  - support-mode rows are aligned.

  This covers the `--tokenizer-worker-num 8` run, which exercises per-request routing.

Builds on the sampling-mask work in #36630, #36631, and #40932.
